sections.title: Verify It Works
sections.html:
Testing the pack on an Android device

Run this once, after copying the files across, before you depend on it. Roughly ten minutes. Each test has a concrete checkpoint — a number to match, not a vague "does it seem OK".

Tests are ordered so that a failure tells you where the problem is. If a test fails, stop and fix it before moving on — later tests assume the earlier ones passed.

Test 1 — The transfer completed

Why first: a truncated download or a partial extract explains almost every later symptom, and looks like something else.

In your file manager, open Download/cysa-plus-study/ and check:

CheckExpected
Visible files in the root folder19 — 15 .md, 2 .py, 1 .html, 1 .sha256 — plus the audio folder
cysa-offline.html~160 KB
audio/ contains8 .mp3, playlist.m3u, and a narration/ folder
audio/ total size~24 MB

Fails if: the folder is missing files, or cysa-offline.html is under 150 KB. Re-download the zip and extract again — most likely the extract was interrupted.

Optional: verify byte-for-byte

If you have Termux installed:

cd /sdcard/Download/cysa-plus-study
sha256sum -c checksums.sha256

Every line should read OK. This is the only test that proves the files are

identical, not merely present. Skip it if you don't already use Termux — the size checks above catch real-world corruption.

Test 2 — Audio plays, and is complete

Open audio/ in VLC or AntennaPod. Check each track's total length against this table — a track that plays but is short was truncated in transfer.

TrackExpected length
01-security-operations.mp322:04
02-vulnerability-management.mp320:42
03-incident-response.mp311:14
04-reporting-communication.mp38:58
frameworks.mp34:01
tools-reference.mp36:34
acronyms.mp37:32
flashcards.mp324:02
Total1:45:11

Fails if: tracks don't appear at all → Android's media scanner hasn't indexed them. Open the folder once in VLC, or reboot. This is not a file problem.

Test 3 — The flashcard drill has its gaps

This is the one feature that can break silently, so it gets its own test.

Play audio/flashcards.mp3 from the start. You should hear:

  1. An intro: "Flashcard Drill. 92 cards…"
  2. At about 0:12, the first question ends and a 3-second silence begins
  3. At about 0:16, the answer starts: "Answer. Four six two four…"
  4. The next question at roughly 0:29, the one after at 0:43

Fails if: the answer follows the question immediately with no pause. The file was re-encoded by something in transit, or you're playing a different build. Re-copy from the zip.

Also check: playback speed is at 1.0×. At 1.5× the gap is 2 seconds, which isn't long enough to retrieve an answer — the drill stops working as a drill.

Test 4 — The written pack renders

Tap cysa-offline.html → Open with → Chrome.

CheckExpected
Contents buttonA ☰ Contents button, top-left
Tapping itA sidebar slides in listing 13 sections
Tap "3. Incident Response"Jumps to that section
The order-of-volatility listNumbered 1–7, readable
Domain 1's logging tableScrolls sideways on its own without the page scrolling
Command Cheatsheet sectionCode blocks in a monospace font, scrolling sideways
Page bodyDoes not scroll sideways at any point

Fails if: the page is unstyled black-on-white text → the file is truncated; recheck its size in Test 1.

Dark mode

Switch the phone to dark theme (Settings → Display → Dark theme) and reload. The page should follow — dark background, light text, tables still legible. Switch back and it should follow again.

Test 5 — It genuinely works offline

The test that matters. Everything above can pass while the files are still cloud placeholders that fetch on open.

  1. Turn on airplane mode. Confirm Wi-Fi and mobile data are both off.
  2. Play one minute of flashcards.mp3. It should start instantly.
  3. Open cysa-offline.html in Chrome. Scroll to Domain 3 and confirm the tables still render.
  4. Tap two sidebar links.
  5. Turn airplane mode off.

Fails if: anything spins, stalls, or shows an error. The files aren't local. If you used OneDrive, mark them Make available offline; better, copy them into device storage directly.

Chrome may show a "no internet" banner on a file:// page. That's Chrome being noisy about the network, not about the page. If the content renders, the test passed.

Test 6 — It survives a reboot

Cheap and worth doing. Some file managers extract to a cache directory that Android clears on its own.

  1. Reboot the phone.
  2. Open Download/cysa-plus-study/ — everything should still be there.
  3. Play ten seconds of any track.

Fails if: the folder is gone or thinned out → it was extracted somewhere temporary. Re-extract to Internal Storage/Download/, not to an app's cache.

Quick pass/fail record

#TestPass
1Transfer complete — 19 root files, HTML ~160 KB, audio ~24 MB☐
2All 8 tracks present, total 1:45:11☐
3Flashcard gaps: first pause at ~0:12, ~3 seconds long☐
4HTML renders — sidebar, tables scroll, dark mode follows☐
5Airplane mode: audio and HTML both work☐
6Survives reboot☐

All six pass and the pack is genuinely yours, offline, permanently.

If you rebuild the audio

Regenerating with a better voice (see AUDIO.md) changes every track's length and every checksum, so Tests 1–3 no longer match this document. Regenerate the checksums at the same time:

find . -type f ! -path './.git/*' ! -name 'checksums.sha256' | sort | xargs sha256sum > checksums.sha256

Tests 4–6 are unaffected.

cards.qs: What makes a process suspicious even when the name is legitimate?
cards.as: Its parent. winword dot E X E leads to powershell dot E X E is malicious regardless of names; svchost dot E X E not parented by services dot E X E is masquerading.

cards.q: What is beaconing and how do you spot it?
cards.a: Regular-interval callbacks to C2. Look for tight interval clustering and consistent byte counts; discriminate from update checkers by destination reputation
cards.qs: What is beaconing and how do you spot it?
cards.as: Regular-interval callbacks to command and control. Look for tight interval clustering and consistent byte counts; discriminate from update checkers by destination reputation.

cards.q: What does SPF verify?
cards.a: That the sending IP is authorised to send for the envelope-sender domain
cards.qs: What does S P F verify?
cards.as: That the sending IP is authorised to send for the envelope-sender domain.

cards.q: What does DKIM verify?
cards.a: A cryptographic signature proving the message wasn't altered in transit
cards.qs: What does D KIM verify?
cards.as: A cryptographic signature proving the message wasn't altered in transit.

cards.q: What does DMARC add over SPF and DKIM?
cards.a: Alignment with the visible From header, a policy (none/quarantine/reject), and reporting
cards.qs: What does D MARK add over S P F and D KIM?
cards.as: Alignment with the visible From header, a policy (none or quarantine or reject), and reporting.

cards.q: Which direction do you read a Received: header chain?
cards.a: Bottom to top — the bottom-most Received is the origin
cards.qs: Which direction do you read a Received: header chain?
cards.as: Bottom to top, the bottom-most Received is the origin.

cards.q: What's the classic BEC header tell?
cards.a: Reply-To differs from From — the display name looks internal, replies go external
cards.qs: What's the classic BEC header tell?
cards.as: Reply-To differs from From, the display name looks internal, replies go external.

cards.q: Name the Pyramid of Pain levels bottom to top.
cards.a: Hash values, IP addresses, domain names, network/host artefacts, tools, TTPs
cards.qs: Name the Pyramid of Pain levels bottom to top.
cards.as: Hash values, IP addresses, domain names, network or host artefacts, tools, T T Ps.

cards.q: Why detect at the TTP level?
cards.a: TTPs are expensive for the adversary to change; hashes and IPs are trivially rotated
cards.qs: Why detect at the T T P level?
cards.as: T T Ps are expensive for the adversary to change; hashes and IPs are trivially rotated.

cards.q: STIX vs TAXII?
cards.a: STIX is the language for describing threat intel; TAXII is the transport that moves it
cards.qs: STIX versus TAXY?
cards.as: STIX is the language for describing threat intel; TAXY is the transport that moves it.

cards.q: TLP:AMBER means you can share with…?
cards.a: Your organisation and clients on a need-to-know basis (AMBER+STRICT = your organisation only)
cards.qs: T L P:AMBER means you can share with.?
cards.as: Your organisation and clients on a need-to-know basis (AMBER plus STRICT equals your organisation only).

cards.q: TLP:GREEN means?
cards.a: The peer community — but not public
cards.qs: T L P:GREEN means?
cards.as: The peer community, but not public.

cards.q: What makes threat hunting different from alert triage?
cards.a: Hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven; it begins without an alert
cards.qs: What makes threat hunting different from alert triage?
cards.as: Hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven; it begins without an alert.

cards.q: A hunt finds nothing. Was it a failure?
cards.a: No — a hunt that produces a new detection rule or exposes a visibility gap succeeded
cards.qs: A hunt finds nothing. Was it a failure?
cards.as: No, a hunt that produces a new detection rule or exposes a visibility gap succeeded.

cards.q: What is the Admiralty Code used for?
cards.a: Rating threat intel: source reliability (A–F) and information credibility (1–6)
cards.qs: What is the Admiralty Code used for?
cards.as: Rating threat intel: source reliability (A, F) and information credibility (1 to 6).

cards.q: Which tasks are good automation candidates?
cards.a: Repeatable, high-volume, low-judgement tasks with well-defined inputs — enrichment, IOC lookups, ticket creation
cards.qs: Which tasks are good automation candidates?
cards.as: Repeatable, high-volume, low-judgement tasks with well-defined inputs, enrichment, I O C lookups, ticket creation.

cards.q: What's the danger of over-automation?
cards.a: An automated containment action that fires on a false positive can cause the outage the attacker wanted
cards.qs: What's the danger of over-automation?
cards.as: An automated containment action that fires on a false positive can cause the outage the attacker wanted.

cards.q: Recognise: powershell -nop -w hidden -enc <base64>
cards.a: Malicious download-and-execute cradle — no profile, hidden window, encoded command
cards.qs: Recognise: powershell -nop -w hidden -enc <base64>.
cards.as: Malicious download-and-execute cradle, no profile, hidden window, encoded command.

cards.q: SAML vs OAuth vs OIDC?
cards.a: SAML = XML-based enterprise SSO; OAuth 2.0 = authorisation delegation (not authentication); OIDC = authentication layer on top of OAuth
cards.qs: SAML versus OAuth versus OIDC?
cards.as: SAML equals XML-based enterprise single sign-on; OAuth 2.0 equals authorisation delegation (not authentication); OIDC equals authentication layer on top of OAuth.

cards.q: What is a CASB?
cards.a: Cloud Access Security Broker — a policy enforcement point between users and cloud services; discovers shadow IT
cards.qs: What is a CAS-B?
cards.as: Cloud Access Security Broker, a policy enforcement point between users and cloud services; discovers shadow IT.

cards.q: Split tunnel vs full tunnel VPN?
cards.a: Split sends only corporate traffic through the VPN (faster, less visibility); full tunnel inspects everything
cards.qs: Split tunnel versus full tunnel V P N?
cards.as: Split sends only corporate traffic through the V P N (faster, less visibility); full tunnel inspects everything.

cards.q: Why does a credentialed scan produce fewer false positives?
cards.a: It authenticates and reads actual patch level and configuration rather than inferring from banners
cards.qs: Why does a credentialed scan produce fewer false positives?
cards.as: It authenticates and reads actual patch level and configuration rather than inferring from banners.

cards.q: RHEL reports a vulnerable OpenSSH version but the patch is applied. Why?
cards.a: Back-ported patches — the vendor fixes the flaw without changing the version banner. It's a false positive
cards.qs: RHEL reports a vulnerable OpenSSH version but the patch is applied. Why?
cards.as: Back-ported patches, the vendor fixes the flaw without changing the version banner. It's a false positive.

cards.q: Which finding type is most dangerous?
cards.a: False negative — a real vulnerability the scanner missed
cards.qs: Which finding type is most dangerous?
cards.as: False negative, a real vulnerability the scanner missed.

cards.q: SAST vs DAST?
cards.a: SAST reads source without running it (early, more false positives); DAST attacks the running app (finds runtime/config issues, no source needed)
cards.qs: SAST versus DAST?
cards.as: SAST reads source without running it (early, more false positives); DAST attacks the running app (finds runtime or config issues, no source needed).

cards.q: What does SCA produce?
cards.a: An inventory of third-party dependencies against known CVEs — an SBOM
cards.qs: What does SCA produce?
cards.as: An inventory of third-party dependencies against known C V Es, an S BOM.

cards.q: Expand the CVSS base metrics.
cards.a: AV (Attack Vector), AC (Attack Complexity), PR (Privileges Required), UI (User Interaction), S (Scope), C/I/A impacts
cards.qs: Expand the C V S S base metrics.
cards.as: AV (Attack Vector), AC (Attack Complexity), PR (Privileges Required), UI (User Interaction), S (Scope), C or I or A impacts.

cards.q: What does S:C mean in a CVSS vector?
cards.a: Scope Changed — the vulnerability affects resources beyond its own security authority. Always worse
cards.qs: What does S:C mean in a C V S S vector?
cards.as: Scope Changed, the vulnerability affects resources beyond its own security authority. Always worse.

cards.q: What's the score band for Critical?
cards.qs: What's the score band for Critical?

cards.q: What does AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N describe?
cards.a: Network-reachable, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction — the worst possible reachability
cards.qs: What does AV:N or AC:L or PR:N or UI:N describe?
cards.as: Network-reachable, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction, the worst possible reachability.

cards.q: What does EPSS measure?
cards.a: Probability the vulnerability will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days
cards.qs: What does E P S S measure?
cards.as: Probability the vulnerability will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days.

cards.q: What is CISA KEV?
cards.a: The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue — confirmed in-the-wild exploitation. A KEV-listed medium can outrank a non-KEV critical
cards.qs: What is SIS-ah KEV?
cards.as: The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, confirmed in-the-wild exploitation. A KEV-listed medium can outrank a non-KEV critical.

cards.q: Does CVSS measure risk?
cards.a: No — severity only. Risk requires asset value, exposure, exploitability, and compensating controls
cards.qs: Does C V S S measure risk?
cards.as: No, severity only. Risk requires asset value, exposure, exploitability, and compensating controls.

cards.q: Correct fix for SQL injection?
cards.a: Parameterised queries / prepared statements (input validation alone is not the exam's answer)
cards.qs: Correct fix for SQL injection?
cards.as: Parameterised queries or prepared statements (input validation alone is not the exam's answer).

cards.q: Reflected vs stored vs DOM-based XSS?
cards.a: Reflected = in the response to a crafted request; stored = persisted and served to every viewer (most severe); DOM-based = client-side only, never reaches the server
cards.qs: Reflected versus stored versus DOM-based X S S?
cards.as: Reflected equals in the response to a crafted request; stored equals persisted and served to every viewer (most severe); DOM-based equals client-side only, never reaches the server.

cards.q: Primary XSS mitigation?
cards.a: Context-appropriate output encoding, plus CSP and HttpOnly cookies
cards.qs: Primary X S S mitigation?
cards.as: Context-appropriate output encoding, plus CSP and HttpOnly cookies.

cards.q: What is SSRF and what's the cloud-specific target?
cards.a: Server fetches an attacker-controlled URL; in cloud it targets the metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 to steal instance credentials. IMDSv2 mitigates
cards.qs: What is S S R F and what's the cloud-specific target?
cards.as: Server fetches an attacker-controlled U R L; in cloud it targets the metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 to steal instance credentials. I M D S version 2 mitigates.

cards.q: What is IDOR?
cards.a: Insecure Direct Object Reference — changing an identifier in a request to access another user's data. A broken access control failure
cards.qs: What is eye-door?
cards.as: Insecure Direct Object Reference, changing an identifier in a request to access another user's data. A broken access control failure.

cards.q: What's #1 on the OWASP Top 10 (2021)?
cards.a: Broken Access Control
cards.qs: What's #1 on the OH-wasp Top 10 (2021)?
cards.as: Broken Access Control.

cards.q: Buffer overflow mitigations?
cards.a: ASLR, DEP/NX, stack canaries, bounds checking, memory-safe languages
cards.qs: Buffer overflow mitigations?
cards.as: ASLR, DEP or NX, stack canaries, bounds checking, memory-safe languages.

cards.q: What is TOCTOU?
cards.a: Time of Check to Time of Use — a race condition where state changes between validation and use
cards.qs: What is TOCTOU?
cards.as: Time of Check to Time of Use, a race condition where state changes between validation and use.

cards.q: Vertical vs horizontal privilege escalation?
cards.a: Vertical = user to admin; horizontal = user to another user's data at the same level
cards.qs: Vertical versus horizontal privilege escalation?
cards.as: Vertical equals user to admin; horizontal equals user to another user's data at the same level.

cards.q: You cannot patch a medical device. What now?
cards.a: Compensating controls: network segmentation, virtual patching at IPS/WAF, disabling the vulnerable feature, restricting access, enhanced monitoring
cards.qs: You cannot patch a medical device. What now?
cards.as: Compensating controls: network segmentation, virtual patching at I P S or WAF, disabling the vulnerable feature, restricting access, enhanced monitoring.

cards.q: Name the four risk responses.
cards.a: Mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept — and residual risk always remains
cards.qs: Name the four risk responses.
cards.as: Mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept, and residual risk always remains.

cards.q: When can a remediation ticket close?
cards.a: Only after a verification rescan confirms the fix. Remediation isn't complete until verified
cards.qs: When can a remediation ticket close?
cards.as: Only after a verification rescan confirms the fix. Remediation isn't complete until verified.

cards.q: A vulnerability keeps reappearing after remediation. What's the real problem?
cards.a: Process — a stale golden image or config drift, not patching diligence
cards.qs: A vulnerability keeps reappearing after remediation. What's the real problem?
cards.as: Process, a stale golden image or config drift, not patching diligence.

cards.q: Why is scan coverage the metric that gates all the others?
cards.a: Metrics computed over a fraction of your estate misrepresent risk entirely
cards.qs: Why is scan coverage the metric that gates all the others?
cards.as: Metrics computed over a fraction of your estate misrepresent risk entirely.

cards.q: Why not actively scan ICS/SCADA?
cards.a: Active probing can cause physical process disruption. Use passive discovery, or a test environment
cards.qs: Why not actively scan I C S or SKAY-dah?
cards.as: Active probing can cause physical process disruption. Use passive discovery, or a test environment.

cards.q: SLE and ALE formulas?
cards.a: SLE = Asset Value × Exposure Factor; ALE = SLE × ARO
cards.qs: SLE and ALE formulas?
cards.as: SLE equals Asset Value times Exposure Factor; ALE equals SLE times ARO.

cards.q: Name the seven Cyber Kill Chain stages.
cards.a: Reconnaissance, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives
cards.qs: Name the seven Cyber Kill Chain stages.
cards.as: Reconnaissance, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives.

cards.q: Main weakness of the Cyber Kill Chain?
cards.a: Linear and malware/perimeter-centric — poor fit for insider threat or credential-only attacks
cards.qs: Main weakness of the Cyber Kill Chain?
cards.as: Linear and malware or perimeter-centric, poor fit for insider threat or credential-only attacks.

cards.q: Name the four Diamond Model vertices.
cards.a: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim
cards.qs: Name the four Diamond Model vertices.
cards.as: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim.

cards.q: What is the Diamond Model actually for?
cards.a: Pivoting — from one known vertex you discover the others
cards.qs: What is the Diamond Model actually for?
cards.as: Pivoting, from one known vertex you discover the others.

cards.q: ATT&CK structure?
cards.a: Tactics (the goal) × Techniques (how) × Sub-techniques × Procedures (observed implementations)
cards.qs: ATT and CK structure?
cards.as: Tactics (the goal) times Techniques (how) times Sub-techniques times Procedures (observed implementations).

cards.q: What is MITRE D3FEND?
cards.a: A knowledge base of defensive countermeasures, the counterpart to ATT&CK
cards.qs: What is MITRE D3FEND?
cards.as: A knowledge base of defensive countermeasures, the counterpart to ATT and CK.

cards.q: NIST SP 800-61 phases?
cards.a: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
cards.qs: NIST SP 800 to 61 phases?
cards.as: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

cards.q: Order of volatility, most to least?
cards.a: Registers/cache → routing table, ARP cache, process table, RAM → temp filesystems → disk → remote logs → physical config → archival media
cards.qs: Order of volatility, most to least?
cards.as: Registers or cache leads to routing table, ARP cache, process table, RAM leads to temp filesystems leads to disk leads to remote logs leads to physical config leads to archival media.

cards.q: Why capture memory before powering off?
cards.a: Encryption keys, injected code, and live network connections exist only in RAM
cards.qs: Why capture memory before powering off?
cards.as: Encryption keys, injected code, and live network connections exist only in RAM.

cards.q: What is chain of custody and why does it matter?
cards.a: An unbroken documented record of who handled evidence, when, and why. Gaps can render evidence inadmissible
cards.qs: What is chain of custody and why does it matter?
cards.as: An unbroken documented record of who handled evidence, when, and why. Gaps can render evidence inadmissible.

cards.q: What does a write blocker do?
cards.a: Prevents any write to original media during acquisition — you analyse the image, never the original
cards.qs: What does a write blocker do?
cards.as: Prevents any write to original media during acquisition, you analyse the image, never the original.

cards.q: IOC vs IOA?
cards.a: IOC = evidence something already happened; IOA = behaviour indicating an attack in progress. IOAs catch novel attacks
cards.qs: I O C versus I O A?
cards.as: I O C equals evidence something already happened; I O A equals behaviour indicating an attack in progress. I O As catch novel attacks.

cards.q: Why isolate with EDR rather than power off?
cards.a: It stops network-borne spread while preserving volatile memory evidence and keeping the host analysable
cards.qs: Why isolate with E D R rather than power off?
cards.as: It stops network-borne spread while preserving volatile memory evidence and keeping the host analysable.

cards.q: Trade-off of immediate containment?
cards.a: Stops damage but may alert the adversary and destroy volatile evidence; delayed containment preserves intelligence but risks further loss
cards.qs: Trade-off of immediate containment?
cards.as: Stops damage but may alert the adversary and destroy volatile evidence; delayed containment preserves intelligence but risks further loss.

cards.q: Eradication removed the malware but the host was reinfected. What was skipped?
cards.a: Closing the vulnerability that allowed entry — eradication must remove the vector, not just the payload
cards.qs: Eradication removed the malware but the host was reinfected. What was skipped?
cards.as: Closing the vulnerability that allowed entry, eradication must remove the vector, not just the payload.

cards.q: When is reimaging the only trustworthy option?
cards.a: Root-level or kernel-level compromise (rootkits) — you cannot verifiably clean it
cards.qs: When is reimaging the only trustworthy option?
cards.as: Root-level or kernel-level compromise (rootkits), you cannot verifiably clean it.

cards.q: What must be true of a backup before restoring?
cards.a: It must predate the compromise. Attacker dwell time is often weeks, so recent backups may already contain the backdoor
cards.qs: What must be true of a backup before restoring?
cards.as: It must predate the compromise. Attacker dwell time is often weeks, so recent backups may already contain the backdoor.

cards.q: What must be rotated after a domain compromise?
cards.a: Every credential the adversary could reach — including service accounts and KRBTGT (twice, for Golden Ticket)
cards.qs: What must be rotated after a domain compromise?
cards.as: Every credential the adversary could reach, including service accounts and K R B T G T (twice, for Golden Ticket).

cards.q: Why run incident communications out-of-band?
cards.a: If the adversary is in your email or chat, coordinating there hands them your response plan
cards.qs: Why run incident communications out-of-band?
cards.as: If the adversary is in your email or chat, coordinating there hands them your response plan.

cards.q: RTO vs RPO?
cards.a: RTO = how long until service is restored; RPO = how much data loss is tolerable
cards.qs: R T O versus R P O?
cards.as: R T O equals how long until service is restored; R P O equals how much data loss is tolerable.

cards.q: What is a tabletop exercise?
cards.a: A discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario — cheapest way to find process and authority gaps
cards.qs: What is a tabletop exercise?
cards.as: A discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario, cheapest way to find process and authority gaps.

cards.q: What are the three incident impact dimensions?
cards.a: Functional impact, information impact, and recoverability
cards.qs: What are the three incident impact dimensions?
cards.as: Functional impact, information impact, and recoverability.

cards.q: What is dwell time?
cards.a: How long the adversary was present before detection — the headline IR metric
cards.qs: What is dwell time?
cards.as: How long the adversary was present before detection, the headline IR metric.

cards.q: What makes lessons-learned productive?
cards.a: Held promptly, blameless, and producing tracked actions with owners and due dates
cards.qs: What makes lessons-learned productive?
cards.as: Held promptly, blameless, and producing tracked actions with owners and due dates.

cards.q: Root cause analysis: "the user clicked the link" — is that a root cause?
cards.a: No. Ask why the link arrived, why it executed, why it reached the internet, and why nothing alerted
cards.qs: Root cause analysis: "the user clicked the link", is that a root cause?
cards.as: No. Ask why the link arrived, why it executed, why it reached the internet, and why nothing alerted.

cards.q: Name four inhibitors to remediation.
cards.a: MOU, SLA, organisational governance, business process interruption, degrading functionality, legacy systems, proprietary systems
cards.qs: Name four inhibitors to remediation.
cards.as: MOU, S L A, organisational governance, business process interruption, degrading functionality, legacy systems, proprietary systems.

cards.q: Correct analyst response to an inhibitor?
cards.a: Document the risk, propose compensating controls, and escalate the risk-acceptance decision to the business owner
cards.qs: Correct analyst response to an inhibitor?
cards.as: Document the risk, propose compensating controls, and escalate the risk-acceptance decision to the business owner.

cards.q: How long does GDPR give you to notify the supervisory authority?
cards.a: 72 hours from becoming aware of the breach
cards.qs: How long does G D P R give you to notify the supervisory authority?
cards.as: 72 hours from becoming aware of the breach.

cards.q: What belongs in an incident report executive summary?
cards.a: Plain language: what happened, what was affected, what you did, what it means, what's next. No CVEs, no jargon
cards.qs: What belongs in an incident report executive summary?
cards.as: Plain language: what happened, what was affected, what you did, what it means, what's next. No C V Es, no jargon.

cards.q: What's the spine of an incident report?
cards.a: The timeline — timestamps with time zones, correlated across sources
cards.qs: What's the spine of an incident report?
cards.as: The timeline, timestamps with time zones, correlated across sources.

cards.q: Who decides breach notification obligations?
cards.a: Legal counsel — not the analyst
cards.qs: Who decides breach notification obligations?
cards.as: Legal counsel, not the analyst.

cards.q: Why involve legal early?
cards.a: Regulatory duties, and to establish attorney–client privilege over the investigation where applicable
cards.qs: Why involve legal early?
cards.as: Regulatory duties, and to establish attorney, client privilege over the investigation where applicable.

cards.q: What does a high ratio of externally-reported incidents indicate?
cards.a: A serious internal detection and visibility failure
cards.qs: What does a high ratio of externally-reported incidents indicate?
cards.as: A serious internal detection and visibility failure.

cards.q: What does an exception without an expiry date represent?
cards.a: Unmanaged risk — exceptions must be time-bounded with a review date and named owner
cards.qs: What does an exception without an expiry date represent?
cards.as: Unmanaged risk, exceptions must be time-bounded with a review date and named owner.

cards.q: How do you pitch remediation to an executive audience?
cards.a: Business risk, trend direction, and cost — one page, no CVSS vectors
cards.qs: How do you pitch remediation to an executive audience?
cards.as: Business risk, trend direction, and cost, one page, no C V S S vectors.

cards.q: What does recurrence in vulnerability reporting tell you?
cards.a: A process failure (golden image, config drift), not an individual's negligence
cards.qs: What does recurrence in vulnerability reporting tell you?
cards.as: A process failure (golden image, config drift), not an individual's negligence.

cards.q: Why does cyber insurance matter during an incident?
cards.a: Carriers often require prompt notification and may mandate their own IR firm; failing to notify can void coverage
cards.qs: Why does cyber insurance matter during an incident?
cards.as: Carriers often require prompt notification and may mandate their own IR firm; failing to notify can void coverage.
